segments.text: Part B, in this part of the test, you'll hear six different extracts.
In each extract, you'll hear people talking in a different healthcare setting.
For questions 25 to 30, choose the answer A, B or C, which fits best according to what you hear.
You'll have time to read each question before you listen.
Complete your answers as you listen.
Now look at question 25.
Now read the question.
Now, I just have to go through some possible side effects of the gastroscopy if that's
okay with you.
Yes, fine.
First of all, I can assure you that in most cases the procedure is problem-free, but I
have to point out to you some side effects so that you are aware of them before you sign
the consent form.
Is that okay?
Yes, fine.
Right.
Well, some people can have a mild sore throat for a day or two after the procedure, and
if you have been given something to make you drowsy, you may feel a bit tired afterwards
as well. And some people can get a chest infection or pneumonia. But remember, this
does not mean that you will necessarily get these as well.
Okay, I hope not. And on the odd occasion, the endoscope can cause some bleeding or infection
in the gut and can also puncture the gullet or stomach. But this happens very rarely.
I see.
Is there anything that you would like to ask me or go over again or are you okay with
all this?
Question 26.
Now read the question.
Let's see now. Mrs. T. Hawthorne. Date of birth, 4 February 1963. Hospital number
1, 8, 3, 4, 5, 7, 2, Z. She was prescribed Tramadol today, 15th October 2009, given intramusculary
50 milligrams, started on 13th October at 1130. All okay. Maximum frequency every 4 hours,
dose 600 milligrams. Okay, to be administered as required, intramusculately and given by
senior nurse bond.
Question 27. Now read the question.
So, that's all done.
Was there anything you wanted to ask me?
Yeah, I've still got this big gap on the other side.
I remember you said we might do an implant there too, but that it'd mean a slightly different
procedure.
If I remember correctly, you said that you couldn't put one there because of the bone,
but that you could connect it to the tooth next door?
Is that right?
Well, partly.
What we discussed was what we'd do if you lost the next tooth along.
So we'd have to extract that one.
Then you'd probably need a bone graft there so that we could attach two teeth to a new
implant.
The gap you're talking about is where you've lost a big molar.
We couldn't fill that gap completely using this technique because that had put too much
pressure on the implant.
I see. Well, you said the price would be much higher than the one I've just had done.
I guess that's why.
Question 28. Now read the question.
Challenges. I suppose there's positive and you know we have to look for the positives of that.
For me a big challenge really in terms of nutrition is that everybody eats and drinks so
everybody has an opinion on what they are eating and drinking and athletes are no different than
the general population. You know you can hear messages or stories or information coming across
and sometimes that information might be suitable for geopublic on the streets but in terms of
an athlete that's trained in twice or three times a day that cannot often be a difficulty and
you know factor in a couple of other things like you know changes in body composition trying to
gain weight or trying to lose weight. Athletes sometimes struggle with those particular aspects
of things and quite often sometimes want to go for the quick fix and sometimes my messages
are quite often the longer fix type messages and that can be a challenge. So I suppose
for me as a practitioner the challenge for me every day is to make that message real,
it's to make it suitable to the person that I haven't thought of me but also it has to
be relevant in terms of the science behind it. So sometimes the science doesn't really
change so I have to change the message or the way I adopt the message for the individual
and so forth.
Question 29. Now read the question.
Okay, we need to do our debriefing. Any comments about the case, Jackie?
Well, we were late getting started due to a delay in getting the surgical consent to
come in, but I've talked to the junior resident and I think we just had a few crossed wires
there, so it sorted.
Yeah, we were busy in clinic this morning, but we were also delayed getting into this
room because the case before us went over their time, which pushed us back. That's becoming
a regular occurrence with that particular team. I'm going to ask our nurse manager to
adjust their time slots based on the recent history of their cases.
We were also slow to get the portable films from radiology. There were several rooms
requesting films and radiology seemed short-staffed. That's unusual for them but let's keep an
on that and if it happens again raise it as a concern.
Question 30. Now read the question.
In Bed 12 we have Liam Oglevy. Liam's a 45 year old male who was involved in a motorbike accident and was admitted with a frontal lobe contusion.
He's broken his right arm and hand and has had surgery including metal plates inserted into his arm.
He's also got deep grazes on his left knee and ankle and stitches on his right leg and shoulder.
All dressings have been changed this morning at 9 and he's on self-administered morphine
drip as well as an antibiotic drip.
He's had injections to prevent blood clotting and his pain's quite manageable with the
medication he's on.
The doctors requested some observation and testing regarding memory loss, so that's
priority this morning.
His right arms in a cast and he'll need regular monitoring and a physiotherapy sessions booked
later in the afternoon.
is coming to collect him at four. I've just checked his vital signs and is stable with
blood pressure at 135 over 95. It's a bit up so you'll need to watch that.
That is the end of part B. Now look at part C.
